Need to search first.I've written verse-by-verse notes from the commentaries I could read, but there are real gaps. I reached the research tool's usage limit early. So every note below comes from the passages the search tool returned for each page, not from full pages I opened. I couldn't fill these sections:
- **Catholic and Orthodox readings:** I found no commentary from newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org.
- **Prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching:** nothing found.
- **bibleodyssey.org:** nothing found.
- **Wesley's notes, and Lutheran or Pentecostal teachers writing on these verses:** nothing found.

I've left those out rather than guess. Where I name a commentator's church tradition (for example "Gill, Baptist"), that label comes from me, not from the page.

---

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:**
- **Who is speaking?** Older commentators disagree:
  - Benson thinks it is Jeremiah speaking of his own troubles. He says too many lines fit Jeremiah personally for it to be the nation speaking. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-1.htm
  - Keil & Delitzsch say these are sufferings that many godly people of the time went through, not Jeremiah's alone. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-1.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary allows either a single believer whose fate is tied to the nation's, or the nation pictured as one person. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/lamentations/3.htm
  - Clarke and Guzik (quoting Harrison) give both options. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/lamentations-3.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-3/
- Guzik quotes Ryken: suffering is always personal, even when a whole nation suffers. He also quotes Morgan: the prophet identified both with the people and with God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-3/
- **"Rod of His wrath":**
  - Ellicott says the wrath is plainly God's, and notes that God is not named. He adds that the poem has become the "inheritance" of mourners in every age. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-1.htm
  - The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary finds the silence about who holds the rod striking, since chapter 2 names Him again and again. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/lamentations-3.html
  - Gill cites the Targum's wording, "the rod of him that chastiseth in his anger." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/lamentations-3.html
  - One commentary on the same page (it appears in Poole's section) says the Babylonians were the rod God used. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-1.htm
- **The word "man":** the NET notes say the Hebrew is *gever*. It works as a "defeated soldier" or "everyman" figure who can stand for any member of the community, male or female. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Lam&chapter=3&lang=de

**v. 2:**
- Matthew Henry: God's providence led him into the darkness he feared, not the light he hoped for. Even God's people sometimes "walk in darkness." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lam/Lam_003.cfm
- Constable: the darkness of God's judgment, in place of the light of His blessing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-2.html
- Gill: the darkness could be the captivity, or Jeremiah's dungeon. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-2.html
- Benson thinks of the dungeon and the stocks, and of the darkness in Jeremiah's mind during those trials. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-1.htm
- A note quoted on Precept Austin says the verb "drive" is used for herding flocks or leading prisoners of war. https://www.preceptaustin.org/lamentations_commentaries

**v. 3:**
- Poole: God's hand once protected him and now strikes him, and not just once but continually. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/lamentations/3.htm
- Gill: God acts like an enemy who used to be a friend, striking blow after blow. He notes the Jewish commentator Jarchi's reading "only against me." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/lamentations-3.html

**v. 4:**
- Gill: his body was so worn that he looked old. He says the broken bones mean his strength was gone, not literal fractures. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/lamentations-3.html
- Calvin compares David's language about his bones. He says nothing is more dreadful than feeling God is angry with us. The prophet was looking beyond outward disasters to the sign of God's judgment behind them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/lamentations/3.htm

**v. 5:**
- Gill links "bitterness and hardship" with the "wormwood and gall" of v. 19: sorrow as bitter as poison, draining his spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/lamentations-3.html
- The NET notes say vv. 4–6 use the picture of a siege. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Lam&chapter=3&verse=7

**v. 6:**
- Calvin: he lived in darkness as if he had long been dead. That sounds exaggerated, but no words can fully express the sorrow of believers who are terrified by God's anger. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/lamentations/3.htm
- Gill: the Targum reads "dark prison house"; the captivity was like a grave (he cites Ezekiel 37:12). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/lamentations-3.html
- Henry: as dark as the grave, like the long-dead whom no one remembers. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lam/Lam_003.cfm

**v. 7:**
- Guzik quotes Harrison: walling prisoners into tight spaces was a torture the Assyrians made popular. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-3/
- The NET notes say the verb can mean either "build a wall" or "block a road." Verses 7–9 picture an escape attempt stopped by blocked roads. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Lam&chapter=3&verse=7
- Gill: "chain" can be read "my brass" (bronze fetters), and the heavy chain means unbearable suffering. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/lamentations-3.html

**v. 8:**
- Calvin: when God doesn't answer at once, our eagerness to pray cools and almost dies, so this verse is "worthy of special notice." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/lamentations/3.htm
- Poole: he prayed loudly and urgently, but God shut the gate like an official who won't hear petitioners. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/lamentations/3.htm
- Guzik: normally God is our refuge in trouble, but here Judah felt blocked in on every side. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-3/
- The Pulpit Commentary's sermon notes say it is Christ's work to clear away the cloud that keeps our prayers from God. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/lamentations-3.html

**v. 9:**
- Gill: a wall of cut, well-fitted stone, not a hedge. He applies it to the prison, the siege, or the captivity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/lamentations-3.html
- Calvin: "crooked paths" means God frustrates our plans. It does not mean God unjustly leads people astray. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/lamentations/3.htm

**vv. 10–11:**
- Guzik: Jeremiah lists the ways God seemed to attack him, like a bear or lion waiting to ambush. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-3/
- Coffman: the images move from wild animals to a hunter (v. 12). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/lamentations-3.html

**vv. 12–13:**
- Clarke: he felt like a target for all of God's arrows, each one a disaster that reached his soul, with God never missing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/lamentations-3.html

**v. 14:**
- Gill: Jeremiah was mocked by his own people, especially the men of his home town, Anathoth (Jeremiah 20:7). If the speaker stands for the nation, the mockers must be outsiders. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/lamentations-3.html
- Lange says this verse "plainly" points to Jeremiah. Keil & Delitzsch say it does not prove the speaker was a well-known figure. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lange/lamentations/3.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-1.htm
- Calvin: being mocked was a fitting payback for a people who had kept mocking God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/lamentations/3.htm

**v. 15:**
- Calvin on "bitterness and gall": even believers are not free from sorrow and impatience. They struggle with their weakness, and their example keeps us from despair. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/lamentations/3.htm

**v. 16:**
- Coffman takes the gravel as a picture of sorrow. He notes that Cheyne took it literally, of the exiles. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/lamentations-3.html

**vv. 17–18:**
- Lange: vv. 17–18 state plainly what the images mean. God's name appears for the first time only at the end of v. 18, with a "grating" effect. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lange/lamentations/3.htm
- Guzik quotes Ellison: mentioning "the LORD" broke the spell of misery. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-3/
- Calvin: his faith had not just wavered but failed. "I say" means a settled conviction, and God's children sometimes believe they are lost. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/lamentations/3.htm
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: he is talking to himself and has lost his sense of direction toward God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/lamentations-3.html

**v. 19:**
- Calvin: many read this as a prayer ("Remember..."). He prefers to tie it to v. 18, as a description of how close he came to losing hope. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/lamentations/3.htm
- Coffman reads vv. 19–21 as Jeremiah remembering God in his cry for help. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/lamentations-3.html
- Guzik: Jeremiah does not prescribe positive thinking. He finds it useful to remember the pain honestly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-3/

**v. 20:**
- Guzik: it was good for his soul to hit bottom so he could build on the right foundation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-3/
- Clarke: the complaining so far shows a bitterness unfit for someone under God's discipline, and while he indulged it, hope fled. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/lamentations-3.html
- Calvin: take a middle course. Face your troubles honestly, but dwelling on them too much opens the door to Satan and despair. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/lamentations/3.htm

**v. 21:**
- Henry: "this" points forward to vv. 22ff, not back to the complaint. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lam/Lam_003.cfm
- The NET notes give the Hebrew as "I cause to return" to mind. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=lam+3%3A21-24
- Guzik: this is perhaps the first time in the book that hope is allowed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-3/
- A devotional on Precept Austin: memory first humbled his pride (v. 20), then defeated his despair (v. 21). It links this to the "hope in God" of Psalm 42. https://www.preceptaustin.org/a_powerful_principle_hope_in_god

**v. 22:**
- **"Not consumed":** Guzik says a remnant remained, and where God leaves life He leaves hope. He quotes Ellison on *ḥesed* (covenant love) and *raḥamim* (compassion, from the word for "womb"). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-3/
- **Deserved punishment:**
  - Henry: we are treated according to God's mercies, not our sins. The covenant still stands even though Jerusalem lies in ruins. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lam/Lam_003.cfm
  - Poole: we were spared because of God's free love, not because He lacked the power or we lacked the guilt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/lamentations/3.htm
  - Got Questions defines mercy as God holding back a deserved punishment. https://www.gotquestions.org/mercies-new-every-morning.html
- **The wording in Hebrew:**
  - The NET notes say this is the only place where plural *ḥesed* comes before plural *raḥamim*. The traditional Hebrew text (the Masoretic Text) reads *tamnu*, "we are not cut off," which KJV, NKJV and NIV follow, while the NET translates "never ceases." https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=lam+3%3A21-24
  - The Pulpit Commentary prefers the Targum and Syriac reading *tammu*, "they cease not," because v. 23 is parallel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-22.htm
  - Everett notes that Paul House prefers that reading too, and says Calvin argued the context supports it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghe/lamentations-3.html
- **Sermons:**
  - Chuck Smith links the verse to "love never fails" (1 Corinthians 13): God's love depends on who He is, not on us. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-22.html
  - Spurgeon, preaching on vv. 22–23: every new sin is met by a new pardon. https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-novelties-of-divine-mercy
  - Precept Austin collects devotionals on how this verse inspired the hymn "Great Is Thy Faithfulness." https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60785/

## 2. Where Protestant teachers differ

- **Is the sufferer a picture of Christ (vv. 1–6)?** Teachers split clearly:
  - Gill (Baptist) applies vv. 2–4 and 6 to Christ. God's hand of justice struck Christ as our substitute; Christ "looked like one about fifty"; He was literally laid in a dark grave. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/lamentations-3.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary's sermon notes call the man of v. 1 a type of Christ, the "Man of sorrows." Ironside (Brethren) says Jeremiah "may almost be looked upon as a type" of Christ. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/lamentations-3.html ; https://studylight.org/commentaries/isn/lamentations-3.html
  - Lange quotes older writers who call Jeremiah a real type of Christ. It reports that the opening of this chapter was written in Latin on paintings of the wounded, thorn-crowned Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lange/lamentations/3.htm
  - Clarke (Methodist) disagrees: applying these lines to Christ's passion is, in his view, "without any foundation." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/lamentations-3.html
- **Were the complaints right (vv. 18–20)?**
  - Calvin (Reformed): the complaints of holy men are not a rule for us. They spoke "according to the judgment of the flesh." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/lamentations/3.htm
  - Clarke likewise calls the complaining unfitting. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/lamentations-3.html
  - Guzik (Calvary Chapel) puts it more positively: sinking to the bottom was good for the soul. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-3/
- **v. 22, "not consumed": a difference of emphasis**
  - Gill: God's people are not consumed "and never shall" be, because these mercies are eternal and kept in Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-22.htm
  - Clarke states it generally: if any sinner is kept out of hell, it is because God's compassion does not fail. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-22.html

## 3. Other views

- **Modern scholarship (NET notes):** the speaker as an "everyman" soldier (v. 1); the siege and blocked-road images (vv. 4–9); and the Hebrew wording of v. 22 (all with URLs above).
- **Catholic:** Bible Hub's Catholic Bible page gives the Douay-Rheims wording of v. 22, which keeps "we are not consumed." It cross-references Malachi 3:6 and Psalm 78:38. This is a translation, not commentary. https://biblehub.com/catholic/lamentations/3-22.htm
